messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sokha was a 72-year-old Cambodian American man who had come to therapy at his wife’s urging after months of sleeping lightly, flinching at ordinary noises, and keeping himself tightly controlled from dawn to night. He worked as a nanny for his daughter’s young children, a role that kept him in their home most weekdays, where toys knocked against hardwood floors, small bodies darted suddenly around corners, and evening shadowed rooms could leave him uneasy. What he described, though, began decades earlier, in a marriage that had once been marked by private cruelty. During those years, when his partner struck him and cornered him in the dark, Sokha learned to go still, to swallow what he felt, and to endure without protest because any display of anger seemed only to bring more violence. He left that life behind, but not the bodily certainty it had taught him.

Now, when a memory came, it did not feel like a story he owned. He spoke of it as if it belonged to someone else, something distant and foreign, yet the terror returned with full force when he remembered being pinned and afraid, and at those moments his body would tense in the same position he had been in then, as if the old scene were unfolding again around him. Those recollections made it harder for him to tolerate his own anger; he had come to believe that even feeling angry was dangerous, and he forced himself to clamp down on it completely. If he sensed irritation rising, he shut it away at once, fearing that once anger appeared he would lose control or somehow invite harm back into his life. The memory and his fear of what it stirred in him had, over time, taught him that silence was safer than feeling.

That conviction had been strengthened by the way his body now responded to the world. Sokha said he was jumpy and easily startled, especially when someone came up behind him or moved suddenly in his line of sight. In the nannying job, one of the children running unexpectedly past him in the hallway could make his heart leap and his shoulders jerk before he had time to think. He could not relax even in the family’s bright kitchen or in his own living room, because part of him stayed braced for impact. The old terror made his body stay on guard, and the body’s constant tension fed back into the memory itself: a quick movement or a noise would call up the same frozen fear, the same sense of being trapped in that earlier room. When that happened, he tried to regain control by suppressing more than anger; he avoided anything stressful, declined invitations, and steered away from difficult conversations. If the apartment was dark, he moved through it only when necessary, keeping lights on longer than he needed and choosing routes that let him see what was ahead.

Over the months, those habits narrowed his life. He said he had become careful about not letting himself become upset, because even mild stress seemed to leave him more reactive and more haunted by the old scenes. So he avoided arguments, avoided news that felt upsetting, avoided situations that might raise his blood pressure or “wake up” the bad memories. He no longer lingered after work, and at home he withdrew into quiet tasks rather than risk being caught off guard. His wife noticed that he sat stiffly at the edge of family gatherings, scanning doorways and flinching if a grandchild dropped a spoon. Sokha knew these were exaggerated reactions, but he also felt that staying controlled was the only thing preventing the past from overwhelming him again. What finally pushed him to seek help was the growing exhaustion of living that way, and the shame of realizing that the same fear that had once protected him now seemed to be shrinking his world. He hoped therapy might help him feel safe enough to stop bracing for an attack that no longer belonged to his present, though what frightened him most was the possibility that if he let his guard down, the old terror would take over completely.
